paragraphs.source_en: The lowest Holocene level, dated to 9,420+200 BP (calBP 10,726± 300), revealed small stone circles about 3m in diameter, positioned in various parts of the shelter, which were probably the foundations of huts. The inside of the circles was paved with flat stones and covered with the remains of still-preserved plants. It seems that at both Tin Torha and Tin Hanakaten groups did not simply use the natural shelter but improved it by organising the living space in a way that suggests a series of family areas (Hachid 1998). The lithic tools represent quartz microlithics and rough flakes made of local microdiorite, quartzite, basalt and quartz. Grinding equipment is abundant and some stones bear traces of red and yellow ochre. Faunal remains consist of wild animals, mainly mouflon and antelope, but rhinoceros, wild boar, hare, rat, porcupine, grasshoppers and tortoise are also present.

paragraphs.source_en: Seven burials found in various levels testify that this shelter was used as both a dwelling and a burial ground. The oldest level, dated to 9,420+200 BP (calBP 10,726±300), contained a child's skeleton, carefully placed on a funeral litter on his left side in a crouched position. The bodies of three adults were placed in vegetal basketwork coverings coated with kaolin, their heads oriented towards the west. Another skeleton of a child, dating to 7,900+120 BP (calBP 8,771±168), was laying on a bed of wild plants in a chamber made of big flat stones, covered with a pile of stone blocks, rather like a small barrow. Remains of the skin confirmed that the child was dark-skinned. This individual had an abnormally shaped skull with a narrow face and a long nape of the neck, which possibly resulted from an illness.

paragraphs.source_en: However, similar deformation has been noted amongst Nigerian Neolithic people (Aumassip 1989) which suggests a deformation deliberately inflicted for cultural reasons, for example from the application of bandages or other compressive material to the head (Hachid 1998). The osteological study showed that the skeletons could be divided into two types, the first Melano-African type with some Mediterranean affinities, the other a robust Negroid type. Black people of different appearance were therefore living in the Tassili and most probably in the whole Central Sahara as early as the 10th millennium BP (Hachid 1998).
